rules.quote: Grammatical contractions are not generally used in formal content.

when: The content is formal (e.g. high-level briefings or responses to parliamentary questions).

covers.quote: Don’t end contractions with full stops
The exception is when the contraction ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

examples.note: No full stop after the contraction mid-sentence.

parts.quote: Tempo Australia Ltd hired him last year.

examples.note: A full stop after the contraction is allowed when ending the sentence.

parts.quote: He is currently working for Tempo Australia Ltd.

examples.note: No full stop after the contraction when another terminal punctuation mark ends the sentence.

parts.quote: They said they can’t!

rules.quote: Don’t place a full stop after contractions.
rules.violation_condition: a contraction followed by a full stop that does not end the sentence
when: Except when the contraction falls at the end of a sentence and is not followed by another terminal punctuation mark.
rules.why: G-4 prefer body sentence over candidate heading; G-3 exception folded into when.

rules.quote: Don’t use an apostrophe to show missing letters in a contraction of a single word (‘Dr’, ‘Ltd’).
rules.violation_condition: a single-word contraction written with an apostrophe

parts.quote: shan’t

examples.note: Violating double apostrophe in grammatical contraction.

parts.quote: sha’n’t

rules.quote: Grammatical contractions use only one apostrophe, even if the contraction leaves out letters from more than one place.
rules.violation_condition: a grammatical contraction containing more than one apostrophe
rules.why: Distinct rule regarding the number of apostrophes in grammatical contractions.

covers.quote: Capitalise contractions in the same way as the full word

rules.quote: Use the capitalisation that you would use for the uncontracted word.

rules.quote: Write out the contracted term in full unless it’s a grammatical contraction.
